podcast.title: Parody and Copyright Precedent (1956)
podcast.body: Dickie Goodman was taken to court for copyright infringement for his 1956 novelty song "Flying Saucer," but a judge ruled it was parody and therefore a brand new composition, allowing him to continue having hits using this method until 1975. "Goodman was taken to court for copyright infringement, but he was left off the hook when a judge declared that this was parody and therefore a brand new composition."

podcast.title: Commercially Driven
podcast.body: Goodman saw opportunities in popular cultural phenomena, like the movie *Jaws*, and quickly capitalized on them by creating novelty records. He was reportedly laughing and writing material for a new record while *Jaws* was terrifying people. "Goodman said that while jaws was scaring people he was laughing and writing material for a new record."

podcast.title: Pioneer of the Break-in Record
podcast.body: Dickie Goodman is considered a pioneer of the "break-in" record format, which involves mixing snippets of current songs and news reports into a narrative. This technique, though technically challenging in the 1950s and 70s, defined his novelty song style. "His son later said that he believes that his dad was the pioneer of the break in record."
